input: Did any trial measure ambulatory blood pressure?
We randomised 240 adults with stage 1 hypertension at two community clinics to a 24-week supervised brisk-walking programme (n = 120) or usual care (n = 120).
The primary outcome was change in office systolic blood pressure (SBP) at 24 weeks.
At 24 weeks, mean SBP fell by 6.1 mmHg more in the walking group than in usual care (95% CI 3.2 to 9.0). Adherence, defined as attending 70% of sessions, was 64%.
Limitation: participants were recruited in 2018 and 2019, before the 2020 change in clinic referral rules.
WALK-2 enrolled 410 adults (2020-2022) and gave the intervention group a step counter and a weekly text message, without supervised sessions.
The primary outcome was change in home SBP at 24 weeks.
The between-group difference in home SBP was 2.4 mmHg (95% CI -0.3 to 5.1). The authors describe the effect as "small and uncertain".
31% of the intervention group stopped wearing the counter before week 12.
STEP-HTN randomised 186 adults between 2022 and 2024 to walking plus a two-session diet consultation, or to diet consultation alone.
Primary outcome: 24-hour ambulatory SBP at 24 weeks.
Ambulatory SBP fell by 4.0 mmHg more with walking plus diet advice (95% CI 1.1 to 6.9). No serious adverse events were attributed to the intervention.
